MASTER CODEC / 09 OF 19

Shell Scripting

Turn a few commands into a repeatable, readable workflow—with explicit success and failure.

IN THIS CHAPTER

01Commands saved in a file02Quote data, not just commands03A check with an exit status04Repeat a small action05Make automation observable06Try it yourself07Common mistakes

All 19 chapters →

What you will learn

  • Use variables, quoting, loops and exit status.
  • Run a script without replacing the shell or changing PATH.

Before you begin

Ready Linux userland and Chapter 3. Work in a disposable private project folder.

Commands saved in a file

Create greet.sh using the Editor. Run it with bash greet.sh; this does not require chmod or a hard-coded desktop shebang. CodeC’s Bash lives in its own prefix. Never overwrite that executable with a script.

greet.sh

name="CodeC learner"
printf 'Hello, %s\n' "$name"

Run the script

bash greet.sh

Expected output

Hello, CodeC learner

Quote data, not just commands

name=value has no spaces around =. "$name" expands as one argument, preserving spaces. Single quotes keep text literal. A dollar sign in an example is not a terminal prompt to type unless it belongs to the command.

Quoting demonstration

folder="practice notes"
mkdir -p "$folder"
printf 'one line\n' > "$folder/note.txt"
cat "$folder/note.txt"

Expected output

one line

The > operator replaces a file. >> appends; choose the operation deliberately, and never experiment on a valuable existing file.

A check with an exit status

check.sh

if test -f "practice notes/note.txt"; then
    printf 'PASS: note exists\n'
else
    printf 'FAIL: note missing\n' >&2
    exit 1
fi

Run and inspect status

bash check.sh
printf 'status=%s\n' "$?"

Expected after the previous exercise: PASS and status=0. On failure the script prints to standard error and returns1. Capture $? immediately; another command replaces it.

Repeat a small action

loop.sh

for name in alpha beta gamma; do
    printf 'item: %s\n' "$name"
done
count=3
while test "$count" -gt 0; do
    printf '%s\n' "$count"
    count=$((count - 1))
done

Run it

bash loop.sh

Expected output

item: alpha
item: beta
item: gamma
3
2
1

Keep this explicit and readable before making it clever. Updating count is what makes the while loop terminate. A script can call functions and ordinary installed commands; a missing command still fails.

Make automation observable

Prefer a PASS/FAIL line after a meaningful check rather than printing PASS unconditionally. Do not hide all output with redirection while diagnosing. Before a network, package or destructive operation, state what will change and require deliberate user action.

Chapter 16’s automation script combines this pattern with device APIs. It is an owner-device-test gate precisely because shell syntax checks cannot prove Android speech or permission behavior.

Try it yourself

  1. Run all three scripts from the same folder. Expected: greeting, PASS and the listed loop output.
  2. Rename the disposable note and rerun check.sh. Expected: FAIL and status1; restore it afterward.
  3. Add a function that prints one supplied argument with printf. Call it with a quoted two-word string and verify one line.

Common mistakes

  • Spaces around = change a variable assignment into a command attempt.
  • Unquoted file paths can split into arguments.
  • Do not add . to PATH, replace bash or use broad rm commands for practice.
